Abstract—The rise of Web3 and Decentralized Finance (DeFi)
has enabled borderless access to financial services empowered by
smart contracts and blockchain technology. However, the ecosystem’s trustless, permissionless, and borderless nature presents
substantial regulatory challenges. The absence of centralized
oversight and the technical complexity create fertile ground for
financial crimes. Among these, money laundering is particularly
concerning, as in the event of successful scams, code exploits,
and market manipulations, it facilitates covert movement of illicit
gains. Beyond this, there is a growing concern that cryptocurrencies can be leveraged to launder proceeds from drug trafficking,
or to transfer funds linked to terrorism financing.
This survey aims to outline a taxonomy of high-level strategies and underlying mechanisms exploited to facilitate money
laundering in Web3. We examine how criminals leverage the
pseudonymous nature of Web3, alongside weak regulatory frameworks, to obscure illicit financial activities. Our study seeks to
bridge existing knowledge gaps on laundering schemes, identify
open challenges in the detection and prevention of such activities,
and propose future research directions to foster a more transparent Web3 financial ecosystem—offering valuable insights for
researchers, policymakers, and industry practitioners.
I. INTRODUCTION
Blockchains emerged as a transformative technology aimed
at decentralization, transparency, and trustless transactions.
This vision materialized in 2009 with the launch of Bitcoin [1], the first decentralized digital currency enabling
peer-to-peer (P2P) transfers without intermediaries. Bitcoin
marked a paradigm shift, replacing institutional trust with
cryptographic proof [2]. The second major milestone was
Ethereum [3], which introduced smart contracts, expanding
blockchains into programmable platforms for decentralized
applications (dApps) [2]. As adoption grew, so did the broader
idea of decentralized systems, culminating in the concept of
Web3, coined in 2014, to describe a decentralized alternative
to the traditional internet [4]. Web3’s emergence catalyzed
the rise of decentralized finance (DeFi)—a blockchain-based,
P2P financial system offering alternatives to traditional mechanisms such as lending and investment [5]. As of July 2025, the
global cryptocurrency market cap reached $3.8 trillion, with
DeFi accounting for $135 billion in total value locked (TVL),
demonstrating DeFi’s expanding global impact [6], [7].
Critics have long warned that the unregulated nature of
Web3 facilitates illicit activity [5], including fraud, scams,
wash trading, and code exploits [8]. The presence of highvalue assets continues to attract cybercriminals; in 2024 alone,
$2.2 billion was stolen from Web3 platforms [9], followed
by the recent $1.5 billion Bybit hack in February 2025—
considered the largest crypto theft to date [10]. A key enabler
of such crimes is the ability to obscure the origin of illicit
assets, allowing launderers to integrate them into the legitimate
economy—a process known as money laundering [11]. Frequently associated with drug trafficking and terrorism financing, money laundering is increasingly leveraging Web3 [8],
[12], [13]; between 2019 and 2023, an estimated $93 billion
was laundered via cryptocurrencies [14].
Despite growing concern, crypto money laundering schemes
remain highly diverse and insufficiently systematized. While
works such as Sneck [15], Comolli and Korver [13], and
Almeida et al. [16] provide partial overviews, they often lack
depth, breadth, or up-to-date coverage. Foundational studies
like M¨oser et al. [17], though influential, are now outdated
and omit recent developments. Even more recent contributions,
such as Lin et al. [18], fall short of offering a comprehensive
taxonomy of laundering schemes. A parallel body of work examines only specific laundering vectors—such as mixing services [19], [20], [21], [22], initial coin offerings (ICOs) [23],
cross-chain bridges [24], and non-fungible tokens (NFTs) [8],
[25]. While informative, these studies remain fragmented and
lack synthesis across the broader laundering landscape.
For addressing the above gap, this work delivers a survey
that consolidates known cryptocurrency-based money laundering approaches identified in academic and regulatory sources.
We categorize these approaches by their overarching strategies
and the tools or intermediaries employed, and map them to the
respective stages of the laundering process. Recognizing the
role of data in anti-money laundering efforts, we also examine
the types and sources of data relevant to each approach. We
provide a comparison with previous surveys in Appendix A.
We begin by outlining the foundations of Web3 and
DeFi (§II) and describing our methodology for data collection
and analysis (§III). We then examine how traditional laundering stages adapt to Web3 and the challenges of deanonymization in this emerging ecosystem (§IV). Next, we present
our taxonomy of laundering schemes (§V), including general
obfuscation strategies (§V-A) and intermediary mechanisms
exploited throughout the laundering process to implement
these strategies (§V-B). We conclude with a survey of countermeasures from academia, regulators, and industry (§VI), and
outline open challenges and future research directions (§VII).

II. FOUNDATIONS OF WEB3 AND DEFI
This section outlines foundational concepts essential for understanding Web3 and DeFi. Key topics include the underlying
blockchain infrastructures, classification of digital assets, and
the role of crypto wallets in asset management. Understanding
how value is created, stored, and moved in this ecosystem is
critical for assessing its susceptibility to money laundering.
Blockchains and consensus. A blockchain is a decentralized, cryptographically linked ledger maintained across a
P2P network [26], [27]. To ensure consistency and Byzantine Fault Tolerance (BFT)—resilience to malicious parties—
blockchains rely on consensus protocols [26]. Bitcoin introduced the Nakamoto consensus [1], using proof of work
(PoW) to achieve consensus by requiring nodes to solve
computational puzzles; the longest valid chain is treated as
authoritative [26], [27]. In contrast, Proof of Stake (PoS)
protocols select block proposers based on the amount of
possessed and locked assets (stake), reducing energy use by
eliminating intensive computations. Both models incentivize
participation through transaction fees and block rewards, and
aim to maintain integrity and immutability.
Smart contracts. Conceptualized by Szabo in the 1990s [28],
smart contracts are self-executing programs that enforce predefined rules without intermediaries [8]. Unlike traditional contracts, enforcement is automatic and encoded within the contract logic [29], [5]. Ethereum [3] extended blockchains into
programmable state machines, enabling Turing-complete logic
via smart contracts [30]. These contracts execute atomically—
either fully completing or reverting without side effects [5].
Smart contracts are the foundation of Web3, powering decentralized applications (dApps) and asset exchange [31], [8], [5].
Crypto assets. We adopt the term crypto assets as a unified descriptor for blockchain-based, exchangeable digital assets [32],
[33], where “crypto” denotes cryptocurrency. While alternative
terms such as “digital assets” and “crypto-coins (CCs)” are
also prevalent [5], [34], we use crypto assets throughout for
consistency. This category includes:
Coins and gas tokens. Blockchains such as Bitcoin [1],
Monero [35], and Ripple [36] support a single native
cryptocurrency—BTC, XMR, and XRP—commonly referred
to as “coins,” used as digital currency and for paying transaction or mining fees [37], [26]. In contrast, smart contract
platforms like Ethereum [3], Solana [38], and Binance Smart
Chain [39] use native “gas tokens”—ETH, SOL, and BNB—
to cover transaction costs and smart contract execution [40].
Utility and community tokens. Blockchains with smart contract
support enable the creation of secondary tokens via standards
such as ERC-20 [41] in Ethereum and BEP-20 [42] in Binance
Smart Chain. These tokens may serve functional roles (e.g.,
governance, staking) or may lack explicit utility [43], [44].
Wrapped tokens. These are representations of blockchainnative assets that enable interoperability across chains. Since
assets cannot move directly between blockchains due to isolated state machines, bridges facilitate wrapping by locking
the original asset on the source chain and minting an equivalent token on the destination chain [45], [46]. For instance,
locking BTC can yield wBTC for use in Ethereum-based
protocols [46]. Bridge protocols generally consist of three
parts: a custodian that locks the asset, a communicator that
transmits confirmations, and a debt issuer that mints or burns
the wrapped token [46].
Stablecoins. Stablecoins are digital assets pegged to external
references (typically fiat, e.g., USD) [47], [25]. Unlike volatile
cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin, they aim to serve as stable stores
of value [47]. Stablecoins are classified by [47]: peg type (fiat,
commodities [48]), collateral type (fiat, crypto, commodities,
algorithmic), collateral amount (full, over-collateralized, partial, or none), and stabilization mechanisms. Their stability
depends on collateral volatility, reserves, macroeconomic conditions, and user incentives [49], [50].
Non-fungible tokens (NFTs). Web3 tokens are broadly classified as fungible or non-fungible [8]. Fungible tokens are
interchangeable and divisible, with each unit holding equal
value. In contrast, NFTs are unique, indivisible assets that
function as digital certificates of ownership [25]. Each NFT is
identified by an ID and linked to off-chain metadata (e.g.,
media files) via a URL [51]. NFTs serve as foundational
components of Web3 metaverse ecosystems by facilitating
verifiable, transferable ownership of virtual assets [25], [52],
[8]. Unlike fungible tokens with market-driven pricing, NFT
values are subjective [53], often exchanged through auctions
on platforms like OpenSea [52].
Cryptocurrency wallets. Cryptocurrency wallets are essential
tools for storing, managing, and transferring digital assets
within virtual economies [25]. A wallet enables users to
initiate transactions by signing them with a private key, and
broadcasts it to the blockchain for validation [54]. Wallets vary
by design and provider [25], and are typically classified along
two dimensions [54], [25]: (a) network connectivity, where hot
wallets (e.g., web, mobile) are internet-connected, and cold
wallets (e.g., hardware, paper) are offline to reduce exposure
to cyber threats; and (b) key management, where custodial
wallets entrust private keys to third parties, while non-custodial
wallets give users full control and responsibility. Cryptocurrency wallets are typically initialized using a 12- or 24word mnemonic phrase drawn from a standardized 2048-word
list [55], [54]. These phrases encode entropy and act as humanreadable seeds for private key generation, enabling secure
recovery [55], [54]. Most wallets implement the hierarchical
deterministic (HD) model defined in BIP-32 [56], allowing a
single master seed to produce a tree of key pairs [57]. Protocolspecific derivation paths [58] yield distinct addresses, and the
one-way nature of key derivation makes seed reconstruction or
cross-chain address inference cryptographically infeasible. The
ease of wallet generation facilitates abuse, allowing malicious
parties to create large numbers of wallets [25]. Some networks,
such as Ripple [36], disincentivize mass wallet generation by
imposing a reserve balance requirement.

III. SURVEY METHODOLOGY
In our survey, we primarily used Google Scholar to gather
research from venues in cybersecurity, blockchain, and financial crime. Given the rapid evolution of DeFi, academic literature alone is insufficient for capturing emerging laundering
tactics. To supplement scholarly work, we included regulatory
reports, preprints, books, and theses, spanning the intersection
of topics between finance and computer security. We also drew
on curated SoK resources [59], [60] and contextualized realworld incidents via reputable news sources and blogs.
We queried Google Scholar using keyword sets such as
“Cryptocurrency money laundering,” “AML in Web3,” “crypto
laundering,” “DeFi money laundering,” “mixing services,”
and related terms. These searches yielded over 50 published
academic papers and preprints. Key articles were selected
based on relevance, citation count, and venue, and forward
citation analysis was used to identify additional sources. Given
our work’s interdisciplinary scope, we expanded our search
to finance literature via our university’s library, guided by a
subject librarian. This resulted in the finding of additional
studies, expanding our reference pool to over 150 sources.
We shortlisted articles based on titles, followed by screening abstracts and introductions. Final selections were made
after reviewing core technical sections. Many of these works
cited non-peer-reviewed sources, including publications from
industry, financial watchdogs (e.g., FinCEN, Interpol), and
annual reports from forensic firms such as Chainalysis [61],
Elliptic [62], Mandiant [63], and Merkle Science [64].
To construct our taxonomy, we began by listing all laundering approaches identified in the literature, supplementing
each with domain-specific sources to enhance coverage and
accuracy. Then, we derived a top-down model that organizes
techniques into six overarching strategies, each supported by
specific intermediaries and enablers grouped into two categories and eleven distinct elements (see Figure 1). To ensure
completeness, we extended our investigation beyond academic
literature, identifying emerging techniques not previously
documented—see Appendix A. We also synthesized countermeasures from academic, regulatory, and industry sources,
classifying prevention and detection strategies by approach and
scope to complement our analysis and provide an overview of
defenses aimed at tackling crypto money laundering.
IV. PRIMER ON CRYPTO MONEY LAUNDERING
Money laundering is the process of concealing the illicit origins of criminal proceeds to make them appear legitimate [8],
[13]. By obscuring financial trails, money laundering enables
offenders to integrate unlawful gains into the legal economy
while concealing the underlying crimes and perpetrators [11],
[65]. This often involves transforming assets, transferring them
across jurisdictions, or layering transactions [13]. A big concern with Web3 is its exploitation for money laundering [15].
The pseudonymity of cryptocurrency transactions hampers
regulatory and law enforcement efforts by obscuring the
origin/destination of funds. Criminals often favor decentralized
services over centralized ones with AML controls [11]. Crypto
money laundering is also used to integrate proceeds from
Web3-native crimes such as scams and hacks [13], [8].
Money laundering stages. The money laundering process
is traditionally divided into three primary stages: placement,
layering, and integration (PLI) [13], [15], [12], [25], [29].
Placement. This initial stage introduces illicit funds into the
financial system. Offenders often convert cash into legitimatelooking assets to avoid suspicion, using techniques like
“smurfing”—breaking large sums into smaller, less conspicuous transactions [15], [25]. As the first point of contact with
regulated systems, placement is both critical and risky [66],
[25]. In Web3, placement generally involves converting illicit
fiat into crypto assets (§II), often via loosely regulated centralized exchanges (CEXs) to evade detection [15], [13].
Layering. This stage follows placement and involves fabricating transaction records to conceal the origin of illicit
funds [25], typically through a series of complex transactions
designed to distance the assets from their source [15]. In Web3,
this often involves employing obfuscation strategies (discussed
in §V-A) that reduce funds’ traceability.
Integration. This final stage reintroduces laundered funds into
the legitimate economy, facilitating their use without arousing
suspicion [15]. This stage often entails the purchase of highvalue assets such as real estate, luxury goods, or artwork [15].
Within the Web3 domain, integration may also involve acquiring digital valuables, including NFTs [15]. Moreover,
some frameworks classify “off-ramping”—the conversion of
cryptocurrency into fiat and its reintegration into the traditional
financial system—as a form of integration, particularly when
disguised as capital gains or investment returns [67].
While some scholars have noted limitations of the classical
PLI framework in the context of emerging financial technologies (e.g., mapping specific behaviors to distinct PLI stages can
be challenging with cryptocurrencies) [68], [69], it continues
to serve as a foundational model in money laundering research [13]. We thus structure our taxonomy on crypto-enabled
money laundering around the PLI model, while accounting for
domain-specific particularities. For instance, in certain Web3native crimes such as fraud, theft, or scams, the placement
phase may be less distinct or entirely bypassed, as illicit
proceeds originate within the crypto ecosystem [70], [8]. In
such cases, laundering often begins with layering and proceeds
to integration via off-ramping or asset conversion [14].
The next section examines the pseudonymous nature of the
Web3 ecosystem and its role in laundering, outlines tiers of
anonymity, and highlights a core challenge to deanonymization: limited access to data traces that hampers AML efforts.

B. Typologies of Data for Web3 AML Forensics
The data used for tracing illicit activity in Web3 can be
broadly categorized into two types:
On-chain data. This data type refers to information immutably recorded on public blockchains [13], [75], including
transaction histories, addresses, amounts, fees, and timestamps [73]. Blockchains based on the unspent transaction
output (UTXO) model (e.g., Bitcoin [1]) record UTXOs’
ownership changes, while smart contract platforms (e.g.,
Ethereum [3]) log state transitions, events, and token transfers [5], [76]. On-chain data is publicly accessible through
APIs or explorers like Etherscan [77], Bitquery [78], and The
Graph [79]. However, privacy-focused blockchains (e.g., Monero [35], Zcash [72]) deliberately restrict transparency [73].
Off-chain data. This data type originates outside blockchains,
and is stored by centralized entities [75]. Sources include
CEXs and custodial wallets, which often comply with KY-
C/AML regulations [13]. These entities collect data such as
names, IDs, IPs, device fingerprints, and activity logs [80],
[81], [70] that are accessible to investigators through legal processes. Additional sources include messaging platforms (e.g.,
Telegram, Discord), dark web listings, and communication
logs [70], [82], which provide context on laundering coordination. Analytics firms and regulators also maintain databases
of flagged addresses and known scam networks [81]. While
fragmented and variable in quality, off-chain data is essential
for linking blockchain activity to real-world actors [25].
Notably, cross-chain transactional traces are vital for
detecting asset movement between blockchains—a process
known as chain-hopping (see §V-A3)[18]. These traces are
not separate from on- or off-chain data but may consist of
either—or both—depending on the method used. For example, on-chain smart contract logs from decentralized bridges
(e.g., Wormhole [83], Multichain [84]) reflect token locking,
minting, or burning [45], [67], while atomic swaps using
hashed timelock contracts (HTLCs) [13], [85] or interoperability protocols like LayerZero [86] and Axelar [87] produce
traceable on-chain interactions [45]. In contrast, chain-hopping
via centralized services leaves only basic on-chain deposit
and withdrawal traces, with most linkage data held off-chain
in custodial databases [88]. Finally, some methods—such as
those in §V-A4—generate no cross-chain traces at all.
Tracing illicit asset flows—especially across obfuscation
layers—requires correlating on-chain and off-chain data from
different sources. Each source offers a partial view; only by
combining them can investigators fully reconstruct laundering
paths. Sophisticated actors exploit gaps in data, jurisdiction,
and privacy tools to evade detection [13].

A. General Strategies
In cryptocurrency-based money laundering, most schemes
rely on a core set of tactics to obscure the origin, flow, or
ownership of illicit assets. We group these strategies into six
broad categories. In practice, implementations often combine
or blur these categories, making it difficult to assign a scheme
to a single tactic. Still, our classification provides a systematic
lens for understanding laundering patterns.
1) Transaction
Flow
Obfuscation
(TFO):
Transaction
graph analysis as a means to detect illicit transactions is
inherently error-prone, often yielding false positives due to
the structural complexity of blockchain transactions [74], [29].
Transaction flow obfuscation (TFO) refers to techniques that
deliberately increase the complexity of blockchain transaction
patterns, often by moving assets between wallets controlled by
the same actor, mimicking usual transactional patterns [89],
[90]. As noted in §II, the ability of rapid, low-cost creation of new addresses is often exploited to obfuscate illicit
fund flows [29], [25]. Dispersing assets across many wallets
increases transaction graph complexity and hinders forensic
methods like address clustering [74], [91], [18]. Below, we
outline common TFO patterns (see Fig. 2).
Multi-hop transfers. Chainalysis reports that over 80% of
illicit value flows involve routing funds through intermediary
wallets—distinct addresses placed between the illicit source
and the final conversion service—to increase obfuscation [92].
Each intermediary “hop” represents a transfer between addresses [93], [12]. Multi-hop transfers often form long chains
of “relay transactions” [89], complicating manual tracing, e.g.,
when using public block explorers.
Peeling chain. A peeling chain is a transaction pattern
commonly used by mixing services (§V-B1) to obfuscate
the origin of large cryptocurrency holdings through incremental transfers [74]. It consists of a sequence of “peel
transactions”—each with one input and two outputs [89],
[20]. Starting from a high-balance address, a small amount
is sent to an external address while the remainder returns to
a sender-controlled address [74]. This process recurses until
the balance is fully dispersed, often ending with conversion
at exchanges into fiat or other assets [74], [91], [94]. These
patterns can generate false positives, as they resemble Bitcoin’s
“change address” behavior. Under Bitcoin’s UTXO model,
outputs must be fully spent, and excess funds are typically
returned to a newly generated change address [74], [89]. This
similarity complicates distinguishing illicit from legitimate
transactions [74], [89].
Distributing and sweeping. “Distributing transactions” typically involve any number of inputs and more than three outputs
and are used to split large sums into smaller outputs [90], [89].
They are often associated with a single entity sending funds
to multiple recipients, as seen in gambling payouts or pooled
mining rewards. These patterns, like peeling chains, relate to
smurfing—the practice of breaking large amounts into smaller
units to avoid detection [25]. In contrast, “sweep transactions”
consolidate multiple inputs into a single output [89]. Commonly used by organizations for audit transparency or fund
management, they are also employed to aggregate stolen assets
from compromised wallets [90], [89].
Dusting. Dusting term originally refers to the practice of sending negligible amounts of cryptocurrency—called “dust”—to
multiple wallets to trace and de-anonymize users by monitoring subsequent UTXO spending [95], [96], [97]. It is employed
by malicious actors for extortion, by law enforcement for
investigations, and by analytics firms for research [96]. In
account-based systems like Ethereum, dusting has evolved
into a phishing technique, where adversaries send counterfeit
tokens embedded with malicious smart contracts. Interacting
with these tokens—for example, through swaps or approvals—
can lead to wallet compromise [97]. Dusting is also used for
“address poisoning”, a phishing scheme in which attackers
send small transactions from addresses resembling a victim’s
address (e.g., with matching initial and final characters) [98].
These addresses appear in transaction histories, increasing the
chance of accidental reuse and misdirected funds.
Although not categorized as an explicit obfuscation attempt,
in October 2018, the BestMixer.io mixer sent small Bitcoin amounts to numerous addresses—ostensibly for advertising [22]. However, this act is widely interpreted as an attempt
to disrupt AML systems by contaminating clean addresses,
expanding the anonymity set and generating false positives in
taint analysis (see §VI-B) [22], [71].
2) Commingling: In financial and legal contexts, commingling denotes the intentional mixing of funds from multiple
sources to obscure their origin and hinder traceability [99],
[13], [69]. It was central to 1990s warehouse banking schemes,
where pooled client deposits masked individual ownership,
facilitating tax evasion and money laundering [13]. In Web3,
commingling commonly occurs during layering, where assets
from multiple parties are merged within a shared transactional
or custodial structure. Unlike TFO (§V-A1), where a single
actor moves funds across self-controlled addresses or dusting
recipients without their participation, commingling requires
multiple parties. This shifts pseudonymity to set anonymity,
thus probabilistically assigning fund origins to a group [71].
The terms commingling, mixing, tumbling, and swapping
are closely related in cryptocurrency literature and often lead
to confusion [13], [100]. To clarify, in this paper we use
commingling as an umbrella term referring to the pooling of
assets from distinct parties to obscure their provenance [99].
Swapping, by contrast, involves shuffling transaction destinations to achieve unlinkability [101], [19], [20] (§V-A4). Mixing
is often used as a broader term in the literature, encompassing various actions employed in mixers (§V-B1), including
TFO (§V-A1), swapping (§V-A4), and commingling [101],
[13]. Although the terms mixing and tumbling are often used
interchangeably, some sources distinguish them. Tumbling
refers to fragmenting transactions into smaller parts to obscure
transaction trails [70], [102], placing it under the TFO category
and close to patterns such as peeling chains and distribution.

one chain and release equivalents on another, are also key
enablers of chain-hopping (§V-B4). All such chain-hopping
enablers are detailed in §V-B.
4) Disconnected fund flow (DFF): While previously discussed tactics often leave residual data traces that can support
partial linkage between source and destination account, a
distinct class of techniques—referred to as disconnected fund
flow (DFF) [20], [19]—aims to eliminate any traceable connection between illicit origins and final destinations. And while
earlier tactics typically offer set anonymity [71]—providing
limited resistance to deanonymization—DFF can approach full
anonymity [71] (see §IV-A). Finally, unlike prior layeringspecific strategies, DFF techniques are also applicable during
placement and integration. Below, we explore these tactics.
Disjoint reciprocal transfers (DRTs). A representative example of DFF is a process we refer to as disjoint reciprocal transfers (DRTs), after its structural characteristics—two
reciprocal P2P transactions intentionally designed to appear
unrelated (see Fig. 3). These transactions lack observable links,
rendering their connection untraceable or extremely difficult to
reconstruct, even with advanced forensic tools [21], [16], [13].
Placement via DRTs. In the placement phase, launderers
introduce illicit funds—often in the form of physical cash—
into the cryptocurrency ecosystem via P2P asset swaps with
third parties [16], [13]. These exchanges typically occur
through informal channels such as online forums, encrypted
messaging apps, or social media. The actor transfers tainted
funds to a counterparty, who returns an equivalent amount
of clean cryptocurrency. With minimal contact through safe
communication channels, these exchanges must be protected
against deanonymization. Given the placement stage’s inherent risk [66], [25], [15], launderers exercise caution by
avoiding traceable interactions and leverage privacy-enhancing
technologies (PETs) such as Tor[104] to obscure personal
identifiers and conceal network-level metadata[17].
Layering via DRTs. Layering can leverage DRTs, enabling
a malicious actor (Mallory) to exchange tainted cryptocurrency for ostensibly clean assets from a third party (Alice)
without leaving discernible links. When both transaction happen on the same blockchain, both parties must use distinct
addresses for sending and receiving (Mallory0 →Alice0,
Alice1 →Mallory1), since reusing any address exposes linkages. Related work on stealth address schemes similarly seeks
to preserve recipient anonymity by rendering repeated payments unlinkable [57]. Furthermore, DRTs can facilitate chainhopping (§V-A3). While requesting address changes may raise
suspicion in single-chain transfers, it appears natural when
assets are exchanged across blockchains—e.g., Bitcoin for
USDT. As discussed in §II, addresses on different blockchains,
particularly those derived from hierarchical deterministic (HD)
wallets [58], are structurally unrelated. This address discontinuity breaks implicit links.
Integration via DRTs. DRTs can also serve as conduits for reintroducing laundered assets into the legitimate economy [16].
Adversaries may employ layered crypto assets to acquire highvalue goods—such as real estate, vehicles, luxury commodities, or high-end NFTs—through transactions with legitimate
third parties, thereby completing the laundering cycle.
Related to DRTs are over-the-counter (OTC) and P2P
trades [13], [15], often facilitated by CEXs, such as KuCoin’s
P2P interface for USD–USDT swaps [105]. Here, the platform
acts as an intermediary, connecting laundering actors with third
parties. However, CEXs involvement introduces a degree of
transparency that can undermine the disjoint nature of the
transaction. While CEXs retain transactional records and are
subject to KYC and AML regulations [13], malicious actors
often exploit regulatory gaps to avoid identification (§V-A6).
Swapping. Swapping is also a DFF technique that shuffles
transaction destinations to achieve unlinkability by decoupling user inputs and outputs, thereby preserving address
anonymity [101], [19], [20]. For instance, a swap can map

Zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs). ZKPs are protocols that
let one party prove a statement’s validity to another without revealing underlying information [106], [107]. Privacyfocused cryptocurrencies (e.g., Zerocash [108]) adopted ZKPs
to balance transparency, security, and efficiency [13], [20],

5) Exploit Subjective Valuations: Consider colluding malicious actors, Mallory and Darth. To obscure a $50,000 illicit
payment, Mallory initially acquires a low-value artwork (e.g.,
$50) and orchestrates its resale through collusive bidding
to artificially inflate its price. Darth subsequently purchases
the piece for $50,050, legitimizing the transaction by attributing the overpayment to sentimental value. Mallory, in
turn, justifies the windfall as a capital gain, thereby laundering the funds under the guise of a legitimate art sale.
The subjective nature of art valuation shields both parties
from direct legal scrutiny [109], [110]. FATF’s 2023 report
underscores how the art market’s opacity and lax regulation
enable such exploitation [111]. Unlike fungible assets (e.g.,
fiat, gold), which are uniformly priced, non-fungible assets are
unique, with volatile and opaque valuations. NFTs (§V-B6)
brought subjective valuation into the digital realm, enabling
laundering [25], [112], [113]. A prominent example is The
Merge, which sold for $91.8 million [114].
6) Exploit Regulatory Gaps: Exploiting regulatory gaps is
a core strategy in crypto money laundering [34]. Launderers
leverage inconsistent AML enforcement across jurisdictions,
exploiting regulatory fragmentation to move illicit funds [13],
[34]. KYC regulations are central to AML compliance, requiring service providers and exchanges to verify identities,
monitor transactions, and report suspicious activity [13], [25],
[115]. However, many offshore or non-compliant cryptocurrency services lack KYC controls, enabling anonymous transactions and regulatory evasion [13]. Regulatory arbitrage is a
tactic where launderers shift operations to jurisdictions with
lax AML oversight, exploiting systemic gaps and hindering
international enforcement [13], [115]. The global expansion
of decentralized financial ecosystems and VASPs in regions
with inconsistent regulation, such as parts of Asia-Pacific and
Latin America, amplifies these risks [115].
B. Intermediary Mechanisms
While general laundering strategies in the Web3 ecosystem (§V-A) address high-level tactics for obscuring the provenance of illicit assets, a critical enabler of these strategies lies
in the exploitation of specific intermediary mechanisms. These
intermediaries—including PETs as well as repurposed decentralized infrastructures and financial instruments—function as
infrastructural conduits that facilitate the placement, layering,
and integration stages of money laundering. In this section, we
systematically examine the principal intermediary mechanisms
exploited in crypto money laundering, analyzing how they
are either purpose-built or opportunistically repurposed to enhance obfuscation, frustrate traceability, and evade regulatory
scrutiny across diverse laundering schemes.
1) Mixing Services: Mixing services—also known as tumblers, cryptocurrency mixers, or coin mixing services—are the
primary transaction anonymity tools in Web3. They have been
widely studied across business, finance, computer science, and
legal fields [116], [22], [13], [34], [21], [18].
Mixers emerged shortly after Bitcoin, reflecting early concerns over transaction privacy [17]. Services like BitLaundry [117] and Bitcoin Fog [118] pooled and redistributed
funds to conceal provenance. Bitcoin’s ties to illicit marketplaces boosted demand for mixers [29], which became key
to laundering darknet and ransomware proceeds [119]. From
2015 to 2017, mixer transaction volumes quadrupled [119],
highlighting their role in the crypto economy.
Layering via Mixers. Mixers commonly employ TFO patterns (§V-A1), distorting transaction paths and hinder taint
analysis [19], [74]. Notably, tumbling—breaking funds into
smaller sums to obscure the transaction trail—is a canonical
TFO pattern. This is why mixers are often referred to as
tumblers [70], [102]. Historically, commingling was also a
foundational concept of mixers [13]. Early implementations
exploited Bitcoin’s UTXO model to sever address ownership
linkage [29]. CoinJoin [120], for instance, allowed multiple
users to aggregate UTXOs into a single transaction, making
input-output associations difficult. Modern mixers retain this
principle, pooling transactions from multiple parties and redistributing them to obscure traceability [19], [17]. As discussed
in §IV-A, mixers enhance set anonymity [71], complicating
the tracing of funds back to true sources [19].
Modern mixers also utilize advanced DFF techniques
(§V-A4), such as ZKPs, to obscure fund flows, sever senderreceiver linkages, and hinder taint analysis [19]. As noted
by Wu et al. [101], mixers generally follow two paradigms:
obfuscation (see §V-A1) and swapping (see § V-A4).
Mixing across blockchain platforms enables chain-hopping.
Services like ShapeShift enabled crypto swaps without custodial risk [101], [20], but also facilitated chain-hopping. A Wall

in laundered assets [20].

2) Anonymity-Enhanced Cryptocurrencies (AECs): Some
blockchains are designed to obscure transaction details, including sender/receiver pairs and amounts [13], [71]. AECs—also
known as “privacy coins”—employ advanced privacy technologies that go beyond standard pseudonymity, offering
stronger anonymity. This impedes forensic analysis and can
be exploited to facilitate money laundering [34].
Layering via AECs. AECs support the layering stage by severing links between illicit funds and their origins [13], using various privacy techniques. Monero [35] employs ring signatures,
stealth addresses, and confidential transactions to anonymize
identities and amounts [71], mixing real inputs with decoys
to implement DFF(§V-A4). Zerocash[108], implemented in
Zcash [72], uses zk-SNARKs for fully anonymous transactions;
Zcash supports both transparent and shielded modes, the latter
hiding inputs, outputs, and amounts [71], thereby achieving
DFF. In contrast, Dash [121] applies CoinJoin to merge
multiple users’ transactions, obscuring individual trails by
commingling (§V-A2) [29].
3) Cryptocurrency Exchanges: Cryptocurrency exchanges
are pivotal in the Web3 ecosystem, enabling conversions
between fiat and various crypto assets [13]. Their central role
makes them exploitable across all money laundering stages:
placement, layering, and integration [13], [25].
Centralized exchanges (CEXs). CEXs act as intermediaries
for asset trading [13], managing users’ assets via internal
custodial wallets [25] funded with fiat or cryptocurrencies.
Placement via CEXs. As crypto ecosystem gatekeepers, CEXs
are frequently exploited for placement in weak regulation
settings (§V-A6) [13]. Criminals leverage offshore and no-
KYC exchanges to convert illicit fiat into crypto, often using
smurfs or money mules—multiple accounts depositing smaller
amounts to avoid suspicion [13], [67]. Integrated P2P and
OTC services within CEXs [105] facilitate DRTs, enabling
fiat-to-crypto conversions(§V-A4) that disconnects fund flows
by exploiting regulatory gaps [67], [92].
Layering via CEXs. Many CEXs support off-chain internal
transfers between user accounts [122], [123], [124], [125],
[126], typically free, functioning as simple database operations. These enable off-chain fund movements, with no onchain traces. In lax compliance settings where KYC measures
are absent, such movements evade both on-chain and off-chain
tracing, contributing to DFF (§V-A4). CEXs also facilitate
chain-hopping (§V-A3) by allowing users to deposit assets
on one blockchain and withdraw on another [67]. Finally,
while most reputable exchanges now assign unique deposit
addresses to each user powered by HD wallets, there have been
instances where exchanges have reused addresses across multiple users [127], [128]. This contributes to obfuscating transaction flows (§V-A1) when conducting taint analysis [127], as
well as aggregating funds from multiple users in one place,
inherently contributing to commingling (§V-A2).
Integration via CEXs. CEXs may serve as off-ramps for converting laundered crypto-assets into fiat, reintroducing them
into the traditional economy [25], [92], [18]. In jurisdictions
with KYC/compliance gaps, OTC brokers offer launderers
low-risk fiat exit points [92].
Decentralized
exchanges
(DEXs).
DEXs
operate
autonomously via smart contracts, without centralized intermediaries [33], [13]. They automatically match users trading virtual
assets. Beyond individual DEXs, aggregators synchronize with
multiple platforms, pulling order book data to automate trades
and offer best pricing [13]. As DEXs do not interface with
fiat, their laundering utility is mostly limited to layering.
Layering via DEXs. Launderers employ TFO by exchanging
tainted assets across liquidity pools [18], [129]. Atomic crosschain swaps [103], [93] enable chain-hopping (§V-A3), allowing assets to traverse multiple blockchains with minimal
traceability [129], [67], [13].
4) Cross-chain Bridges: These bridges enable interoperability between isolated blockchains, transferring assets, data,
and messages [24], [130]. They typically use (a) lock-andmint/burn-and-release or (b) liquidity-pool-based models to
manage cross-chain flows [46], [130]. In the former, tokens are
locked (reversible) or burned (irreversible) on the source chain,
while equivalent wrapped tokens (see §II) are minted on the
destination [46]. Liquidity-pool-based bridges bypass wrapped
tokens, executing swaps using pools of original assets.
Bridging also applies to non-fungible tokens [131]. Bridged
NFTs are NFTs transferred across chains via a similar lockand-mint logic as described above.
Layering via bridges. Bridges enable layering by facilitating
chain-hopping (§V-A3) [18], [129], allowing launderers to
move assets across blockchains and sever direct provenance
links [24], thus making it more difficult to trace these assets [130], [132]. Past studies reveal that a substantial portion
of cross-chain fund flows reaches exchanges, highlighting
the operational integration of bridge-based chain-hopping into
broader laundering pipelines [24]. Since NFT bridges facilitate
the transfer of NFTs between blockchain networks [131], they
might also be used to facilitate chain-hopping (§V-A3).
5) DeFi Mechanisms: DeFi comprises primitives such as
lending platforms, yield aggregators, and stablecoins, many of
which can be exploited to add a extra layer of obfuscation
in transaction flows [13], [5]. Although DeFi’s decentralized
8
nature and lack of fiat interaction limit its role in placement
and integration, custodial stablecoin issuers extend DeFi’s
reach to these stages [47].
Loan providers. Decentralized lending protocols facilitate
permissionless borrowing through two primary mechanisms:
over-collateralized loans and flash loans [5], [133]. Overcollateralized loans resemble traditional debt arrangements,
requiring users to lock assets exceeding the loan value. In
contrast, flash loans allow users to borrow assets without
collateral, under the condition that the borrowed amount is
repaid within the same blockchain transaction. If the repayment condition is not met, the transaction is reverted.
Layering via over-collateralized loans. Illicit assets can be
pledged as collateral to obtain clean loaned funds [5]. Furthermore, by extending loans to third parties and receiving
repayments, launderers facilitate commingling (§V-A2) of illicit and legitimate assets. Cross-chain lendings further support
obfuscation via chain-hopping (§V-A3) [130]. Layering via
flash loans. Launderers can acquire flash loans and execute
complex transactions within a single block, including wash
trading—fake trades used as cover—and cycling assets before
repaying the loan [133], [13]. Flash loans can also facilitate
collateral swapping or the repayment of loans with different
assets. These activities can result in TFO (§V-A1) and the
commingling of illicit funds with loaned assets (§V-A2).
Yield farming and liquidity pools. Yield farming refers to
the practice of providing capital to DeFi protocols in exchange
for financial rewards, typically in the form of governance or
utility tokens [33], [5]. A key mechanism for this is liquidity
provisioning to Automated Market Makers (AMMs), which
replace traditional order books by enabling token swaps in
DEXs through algorithmically managed liquidity pools [134].
Users who supply assets to these pools earn a share of the
transaction fees and may also receive protocol incentives.
Yield farming can occur in both decentralized and custodial
manners (eg., through CEXs).
Layering via yield farming. Launderers invest tainted assets
into yield farming to acquire rewards, commingling (§V-A2)
illicit funds with clean proceeds [18], [129]. Rewards may
be withdrawn on other blockchains—when using CEXs—
facilitating chain-hopping (§V-A3).
Layering via liquidity pools. Launderers begin by creating
fake tokens [18], which they pair with legitimate assets—
such as ETH—within DEXs. This pairing involves supplying
both assets to a new liquidity pool, enabling the counterfeit
token to appear tradeable. By conducting wash trades between
accounts they control, launderers simulate organic market
activity and inflate the token’s perceived legitimacy. This tactic
commingles (§V-A2) illicit funds with on-chain liquidity while
masking their origin. Ultimately, launderers extract clean ETH
from the pool, disguised as ordinary DEX trading.
Stablecoins. Stablecoins—especially fiat-backed variants—
serve as gateways between fiat economies and DeFi [49].
Custodial issuers (e.g., Circle [135], Tether [136]) enable the
conversion of illicit assets into legitimate digital dollars, facilitating placement and integration when KYC measures are circumvented. In contrast, crypto-collateralized stablecoins like
Dai [137], which operate primarily as over-collateralized loan
issuers, allow criminals to pledge illicit assets as collateral to
mint new tokens—a process exploitable during layering [13].
6) Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs): Non-fungible tokens were
first implemented on Ethereum via EIP-721 [138] and later became available on Bitcoin through “Ordinals,” which inscribe
arbitrary data onto serialized satoshis [139]. In Web3, NFTs
serve as digital ownership certificates, enabling verifiable
scarcity [25], [140]. NFTs are tightly coupled with Web3 metaverses. The term “metaverse,” coined in Snow Crash [141],
has evolved into a vision of immersive, networked 3D environments. Inspired by MMO games [25], Web3 metaverses
include platforms such as Decentraland [142] and The Sandbox [143], where NFTs represent avatars, skins, and virtual
land parcels. Here, NFTs underpin digital property rights and
enable economic transactions [25]—acquiring metaverse properties often requires only a wallet, bypassing KYC checks [8].
NFTs have been examined as laundering vectors across all
PLI stages [15], [25], [8]. Metaverse platforms—where NFT
trading is prevalent—offer fertile ground for laundering due
to liquidity and ease of transfer of digital collectibles [25].
Placement via NFTs. As described in §V-A4, illicit fiat can be
funneled into NFTs via disjoint reciprocal transfers, introducing tainted funds into the crypto ecosystem.
Layering via NFTs. As discussed in §V-A5, NFT trading with
subjective pricing contributes to layering, while bridged NFTs
also facilitate chain-hopping (§V-B4).
Integration via NFTs. As discussed in §IV and §V-A4, NFTs
can act as value stores or speculative assets [15], and be sold
to reintroduce cleaned funds into the legal economy.
7) Cryptocurrency ATMs and Cards: Here, we explore the
role of ATMs and card-based systems in money laundering.
ATMs. Cryptocurrency ATMs—also known as “Bitcoin ATMs
(BTMs)” [144]—enable access to crypto without online exchanges and can be found in stores or gas stations [13], [144].
To deposit cash and purchase crypto, users provide minimal
ID (e.g., a phone number) and scan a receiver address via QR
code [13], [144]; some BTMs generate paper wallets if no
address is given [144]. For withdrawals, crypto is sent to a
designated address and cash is dispensed.
BTMs have drawn scrutiny for illicit use [13], [15]. TRM
Labs reported that the cash-to-crypto sector—largely driven
by BTMs—processed at least $160M in illicit funds since
2019 [145]. BTMs are frequently used by dark web vendors
to cash out illicit proceeds [13], prompting regulatory concern [145]. Despite existing safeguards, inconsistent regulations and weak KYC measures allow launderers to exploit
BTMs to inject illicit funds into the financial system or retrieve
them as seemingly legitimate assets [13], [15].
Cards. Several card-related mechanisms can be exploited for
crypto money laundering:
Integration via crypto-linked cards. Crypto-linked cards (e.g.,
Visa [146], Mastercard [147]) enable users to spend crypto
9
directly, with issuers converting it to fiat at purchase time so
merchants receive traditional currency [13]. These cards—also
offered by exchanges and payment processors—function like
fiat-funded debit cards, enabling online/in-person payments
and ATM withdrawals [148], [149]. However, they pose laundering risks akin to traditional financial tools [13], enabling
integration of laundered cryptocurrencies.
Integration via gift-card shops. Platforms like Bitrefill [150]
sell gift cards accepting crypto payments, often without strong
KYC policies. During the integration phase, launderers can
convert crypto into gift cards and resell them to third parties.
Placement via pre-funded crypto gift-cards/vouchers. Sold in
fiat, these products are pre-loaded with fixed crypto amounts
and redeemed via embedded private keys or claim codes.
Acquirable in bulk, they can be exploited for illicit fiat
placement, particularly in weak-KYC jurisdictions (§V-A6).
Ballet steel cards [151], [152], Tangem Notes [153], [154],
Casascius/Denarium coins [155], [156], and digital vouchers
from CryptoVoucher, Bitnovo, and Azteco [157], [158], [159],
[160] are notable examples. Although many providers have
discontinued pre-loaded options—likely in response to rising
regulatory scrutiny—such mechanisms remain accessible in
some markets and are considered high-risk instruments [161].
8) Online Gambling Platforms:
Online gambling platforms are key vectors for financial obfuscation and money
laundering [15], [110]. While most accept fiat and crypto,
many crypto-native implementations operate with minimal
regulation [15], exposing laundering vectors across all PLI
stages [162], [161]. Smart contract-based gambling dApps
further automate settlement and bypass AML controls [163].
Placement via gambling deposits. Illicit fiat or crypto is
deposited into gambling accounts as wagers [15].
Layering via gambling activity. Fragmented bets and intraplatform transfers create transaction graphs that mimic legitimate behavior (§V-A1) [16], [15]. Illicit funds mix with
real winnings (§V-A2) [15]. One laundering method is “chip
dumping,” where a player intentionally loses PvP games (e.g.,
poker) to transfer funds to a co-conspirator [161].
Integration via withdrawals. Remaining balances, now masked
as gambling proceeds, are withdrawn to wallets or bank
accounts and misrepresented as legitimate income [13].
9) Initial Coin Offerings (ICOs): ICOs are blockchainbased fundraising mechanisms where ventures issue digital
tokens in exchange for crypto or fiat [164], [23]. Unlike
traditional channels, they use white papers instead of regulated prospectuses and rely on online promotion rather than
underwriting, offering global investor access with minimal
legal barriers [164], [23]. Issued tokens generally fall into
three categories: currency (payment), utility (platform access),
and investment (profit participation), though many are hybrids [165]. The absence of shareholder rights and governance
structures deprives token holders of oversight and heightens
fraud risks [164]. The decentralized nature and regulatory
gaps (§V-A6) make ICOs exploitable across PLI stages:
Placement via ICOs. Placement is feasible when ICOs accept
fiat. Criminals can convert illicit cash into digital tokens. Weak
KYC during early ICO phases [164] facilitated such entry,
though fiat acceptance remains less common than crypto.
Layering via ICOs. More commonly, ICOs accept cryptocurrencies like BTC or ETH. In that case, illegal crypto funds
are invested into ICOs, where they appear as legitimate
contributions to a cryptocurrency project [23]. If the project
succeeds, the funds are returned as profits, now disguised as
lawful investment gains. Essentially, malicious actors invest
tainted funds—commingling them with clean assets of other
participants (§V-A2)—and receive new tokens (§V-A1). If the
ICO sends tokens to a different address than the payer’s, it
introduces DFF (§V-A4). Accepting payments on one network
(eg., Bitcoin) but issuing tokens on another (e.g., Ethereum)
also enables chain-hopping (§V-A3). A more advanced mirroring tactic (§V-B5) is to create a counterfeit ICO, where
actor A hosts the ICO, and B buys worthless tokens using
illicit crypto. The transaction appears as a speculative loss but
facilitates value transfer, exploiting justifiable price volatility.
Integration via ICOs. If a counterfeit ICO accepts fiat, the
scheme extends into integration. For instance, if B invests
in an ICO launched by A and the token later loses value,
B’s crypto is “lost” while A obtains legitimate fiat proceeds,
successfully off-ramping the crypto assets. Projects where developers abandon the protocol without making false promises
are “soft rug-pulls” and may not be considered criminal [166].
10) Consensus Protocols: Recent studies reveal that consensus protocols—particularly Proof of Work (PoW) and Proof
of Stake (PoS)—can be exploited for money laundering and
sanctions evasion [167], [81], [168].
Placement via PoW. Illicit fiat can be channeled into mining
by investing on hardware, electricity, and hosting, generating
fresh crypto that appears clean on-chain—a method reportedly
used by the Iranian government to bypass sanctions [169]. This
approach converts fiat into blockchain-native assets, forming an unlinkable flow (§V-A4). Another Chainalysis report
identified mining pool addresses receiving both ransomware
proceeds and legitimate earnings [167], evidencing ongoing
commingling activity (§V-A2).
Layering via PoW. Mandiant discovered that North Korea’s
Lazarus Group launders stolen funds through cloud mining and hash rental services to acquire fresh, untainted assets [168], constituting a disconnection in fund flow (§V-A4).
Layering via PoS. Launderers may stake illicit funds to generate fresh rewards. The use of liquid staking derivatives (e.g.,
stETH) complicates tracing by embedding rewards into the
asset’s value rather than paid as separate distributions [170].
Staking via custodial or pooled DeFi services also facilitates
commingling (§V-A2) of illicit funds [129]. Launderers may
also withdraw rewards to new wallets, re-stake them, or apply
additional layers using other mentioned techniques.
11) Payment Channel Networks: Payment Channel Networks (PCNs) are off-chain protocols developed to improve
blockchain scalability and efficiency [171], [172], [173]. They
10
enable users to route payments through intermediaries without
direct channels. For example, if Alice is connected to Bob and
Bob to Charlie, Alice can pay Charlie via Bob using hashed
timelock contracts (HTLCs) [12]. Instead of recording each
transaction on-chain, two parties open a bi-directional channel
by locking funds in a multi-signature address, exchange rapid
off-chain micro-transactions, and settle the net balance onchain when the channel closes [12], [19].
Layering via PCNs. Originally developed for scalability,
PCNs have also emerged as effective obfuscation tools in
the layering phase of money laundering. By fragmenting
illicit funds and routing them through multiple off-chain
paths—often via dormant or low-liquidity links—criminals
can obscure transaction trails and complicate attribution [12].
This tactic embodies both TFO and DFF (§V-A1, §V-A4).
Tainted funds may be split across multiple paths and settled
in different currencies, hindering flow reconstruction even
when endpoints are observed [12]. PCNs further enhance
anonymity by recording only channel openings and closures
on-chain; intermediate transfers remain off-ledger [19]. While
most PCNs are confined to a single blockchain—such as the
Lightning Network on Bitcoin [171] or the Raiden Network
on Ethereum [172]—their use of HTLCs and atomic swaps
enables experimental cross-chain capabilities that facilitate
chain-hopping (§V-A3). Notably, frameworks like the Perun
Network propose support for cross-chain atomic swaps [174].
VI. CRYPTO MONEY LAUNDERING COUNTERMEASURES
In response to increasingly sophisticated crypto money
laundering schemes, anti-money laundering (AML) measures
have evolved along two paradigms: (a) detection measures,
which aim to uncover laundering activity (§VI-A); and (b)
prevention measures, which seek to obstruct laundering before
it occurs or prevent its recurrence (§VI-B).
A. Detection Measures
Detection measures monitor and analyze transactional data
to identify suspicious behavioral patterns across the blockchain
ecosystem. Systematically, they fall into the following groups:
Rule-based detection. AML detection has traditionally relied
on rule-based systems, which use predefined thresholds and
expert-crafted conditions to flag suspicious activity [175],
[176]. Conditions such as transaction limits, unusual patterns,
or specific event triggers can be used to generate alerts for
investigation [175]. An advantage of rule-based frameworks
is their interpretability and alignment with regulatory expectations, as institutions must justify flagged activity. Lin et al. [18]
used rule-based methods on Ethereum to trace laundering
paths, while clustering techniques link addresses based on
heuristics like multi-input usage [177], [178]. Firms such as
Elliptic [62], Chainalysis [61], and CipherTrace [179] apply
these rules across chains for real-time AML risk assessment.
However, rule-based systems are afflicted by high false positives, static rules that demand expert maintenance, and limited
adaptability to evolving laundering tactics, making them less
scalable without continuous expert updates [180], [175].
Data-driven detection. Machine learning techniques are used
to inspect complex and evolving patterns in transactional
data [175]. These automate detection, reducing manual rule
reliance and enable adapting to evolving laundering tactics.
Several approaches aim to classify licit and illicit transactions
or entities [175], often employing transaction graph analysis
and addressing class imbalance challenges [175]. Other graphbased approaches [181], [182], [183], [184] model entities
(e.g., users or wallets) as nodes, and relationships or flows
as edges, based on the premise that laundering accounts form
distinct structural patterns compared to legitimate ones. Another line of work [185], [186] frames money laundering as an
outlier detection problem, using clustering techniques to isolate anomalous users and transactions. Gu et al. [187] focused
on anomalous transaction amounts to flag potentially malicious
exchanges. Other studies [188], [189], [190] advanced illicit
activity detection across services such as exchanges, mixers,
darknet markets, gambling platforms, and mining entities by
leveraging transaction histories, address data, and structural
or behavioral features within Bitcoin and Ethereum. Further
efforts analyzed account-level transaction histories to detect
illicit addresses [191], [192], and combined transaction and
account-level insights [193] to enhance fraud detection.
B. Prevention Measures
Prevention efforts focus on regulatory controls, institutional
safeguards, and public engagement, aiming to deter illicit
activity by enhancing transparency. These include:
Regulatory deterrents. Global regulators, led by the FATF,
have extended AML guidelines to Virtual Asset Service
Providers (VASPs)—including exchanges, stablecoin issuers,
DeFi platforms, and NFT marketplaces [12]. The U.S. and the
European Union (EU) have codified these into laws such as
the Bank Secrecy Act and the Fifth AML Directive (5AMLD),
mandating KYC, Customer Due Diligence (CDD), transaction
monitoring, and reporting of suspicious behaviors like smurfing [175]. KYC obliges VASPs to verify identities and flag
suspicious activity. U.S. enforcement bodies such as FinCEN
and the SEC implement these rules, even citing market manipulation risks to reject Bitcoin ETF applications [12]. Consumer
protection is also improving, with the EU’s MiCA and the
UK’s FCA introducing safeguards, e.g., cooling-off periods
for crypto purchases [194], [195].
Promoting public awareness. Crypto money laundering
operates as a complex socio-technical system that remains
poorly understood by users [196]. Launderers exploit this
knowledge gap through fake ICOs (§V-B9), in-person crypto
trades (§V-A4), and gift card sales (§V-B7), often targeting
vulnerable groups such as students and the elderly [197], [16].
In response, governments, industry bodies, and academics
have launched educational initiatives, including workshops and
online awareness campaigns. Notable examples include programs led by the Central Bank of Bahrain (CBB), the Global
Blockchain Business Council (GBBC) [198], and the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) [199].
11
Blocklisting and sanctions. Blocklisting in cryptocurrencies
involves identifying transactions linked to financial crimes
and “tainting” the associated coins [12]. This is feasible in
cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin, where each UTXO’s publicly
visible transaction history imparts a sense of uniqueness and
non-fungibility. For example, the U.S. Office of Foreign Assets
Control (OFAC) sanctioned Bitcoin addresses tied to Iranian
ransomware operators in 2018 [200]. Two primary blocklisting
mechanisms have been proposed [201], [12]: the Poison policy,
which taints all coins in subsequent transactions involving
a blocklisted account, and the Haircut policy, which limits
tainting to the specific coins in the blocklisted transaction.
Additionally, public “taint-lists” have been proposed to discourage engagement with tainted assets [202].
Deanonymization and legal prosecution. As noted in §IV,
launderers exploit the inherently pseudonymous nature of the
Web3 ecosystem, which collectively embolden their use of
cryptocurrencies as a primary medium for illicit financial
activity [71], [13]. In response, government agencies and
affiliated private organizations have invested in improving
deanonymization techniques [73]. These efforts aim to unmask
illicit actors, enabling subsequent legal investigation and prosecution. However, PETs—mixers and AECs (§V-B)—facilitate
anonymity and financial secrecy, prompting technical [119],
[101] and regulatory responses. Centralized mixers like bestmixer.io were dismantled by authorities, while decentralized
ones, being non-custodial and jurisdiction-resistant, evade such
actions [22]. Despite this, OFAC sanctioned the decentralized
mixer Tornado Cash in 2022 for laundering $7B [203]. Privacy
coins face similar scrutiny: Monero was delisted by Kraken
across the European Economic Area (EEA) in 2024 [204],
and will be further restricted under upcoming EU AML
regulations—set to take effect by 2027— banning anonymous
accounts linked to privacy coins [205].
VII. OPEN CHALLENGES & FUTURE DIRECTIONS
We outline core challenges in crypto AML alongside proposed research directions.
Data accessibility. A key limitation of data-driven AML is the
lack of large, reliably labeled datasets [175]. Despite curation,
most labels remain approximate, degrading supervised model
performance due to imbalance and limited coverage [206].
Absence of ground truth raises false positives in detection and
blocklisting, risking collateral damage. Among the data types
in §IV, on-chain data—though public—is vast, noisy, and
ever-growing. Off-chain data face compliance barriers, often
lacking KYC records or imposing access restrictions [13].
Cross-chain traces inherit similar gaps or are entirely missing
(e.g., DRT §V-A4). Constructing transaction graphs entails
fusing blockchain ledgers, smart contract logs, and proprietary
VASP databases, complicating data correlation.
Future directions. (a) Develop semi-/self-supervised models to
reduce label reliance; (b) promote benchmark datasets via joint
labeling by regulators and VASPs; (c) design graph aggregation frameworks for unified, temporally-aligned, multi-source
representations; (d) expand data labeling efforts, building on
prior contributions such as [207], [186], [206].
Pseudonymity and decentralization. Lack of custodianship
limits legal authority to freeze assets or block addresses,
while pseudonymity impedes deanonymization and prosecution. PETs strengthen anonymity, and their decentralized, noncustodial design renders dismantling infeasible. For instance,
in 2024, a U.S. federal appeals court overturned OFAC’s
sanctions on Tornado Cash, holding that its immutable, autonomous smart contracts are not sanctionable entities [208].
Future directions. (a) Promote blockchain infrastructures
which are regulatory-compliant, such as Ripple—partnering
with banks and payment providers to embed AML measures
and KYC protocols into Web3 [209]—and decentralized identity frameworks such as Worldcoin [210], Ethereum Name
Service (ENS) [211] and Polygon ID [212], that support verifiable user and service authorization; (b) Develop legal/technical
frameworks enabling accountable PET deployment and develop compliance-aware PETs with selective disclosure [213].
Regulatory arbitrage. The borderless nature of the crypto
ecosystem undermines AML enforcement. VASPs based in lax
regulatory environments can serve a global user base [13] and
used to move assets across non-compliant jurisdictions.
Future directions. (a) Investigate cross-border enforcement
mechanisms to mitigate fragmentation and propose incentivealigned global AML standards for VASPs; (b) Smart contracts
could embed logic to restrict access from addresses linked
to sanctioned or non-compliant jurisdictions. This can be
facilitated in dApps using compliance oracles that inject offchain regulatory data (e.g., KYC status, sanctions lists, AML
risk scores) into smart contracts (e.g., Silent Data [214]).
Legitimate privacy concerns. Deanonymization efforts further risk infringing the privacy of non-malicious users. PETs
also safeguard legitimate interests—financial autonomy in
authoritarian regimes, commercial confidentiality, etc. Their
dual-use nature complicates regulation, as blanket bans risk
infringing rights and deterring innovation.
Future directions. The development of privacy-preserving
mechanisms such as ZKP-based compliance frameworks (e.g,
Silent Data), and identity systems (e.g, Polygon ID) offers a promising approach. These solutions enable verifiable,
privacy-preserving identities and regulatory attestations, ensuring compliance while preserving user privacy.
VIII. CONCLUSION
This survey aimed to address the absence of a systematized
taxonomy of crypto money laundering schemes, by organizing
existing and emerging strategies at an abstract level and examining their implementations across various mechanisms and
infrastructures across the ecosystem. We highlighted the role
of data-driven forensics and reviewed technical and operational
countermeasures amid persistent challenges. Despite advances,
launderers continue to adapt, casting a pressing need for
scalable forensic tools and responsive policy frameworks to
safeguard the integrity of the decentralized ecosystem.

APPENDIX A
LITERATURE COMPARISON
This appendix compares our systematization of laundering
schemes with prior scholarly efforts that aim to classify
money laundering in the cryptocurrency ecosystem. Table I
(see next page) presents a taxonomy-based coverage analysis,
highlighting the overlap and divergence between our work and
existing surveys.
Kolachala et al. [12] label their work as a systematization
of knowledge paper on money laundering in cryptocurrencies;
however, their primary focus is on money laundering countermeasures, particularly about blocklisting and traceability.
Although they provide a detailed technical analysis of laundering via PCNs and HTLCs, they do not aim to propose a
structured taxonomy of laundering strategies or intermediary
mechanisms.
Lin et al. [18] introduce a modified lifecycle-based taxonomy of money laundering stages in cryptocurrency systems.
While this offers a broad conceptual framing, it leaves out
many laundering schemes.
Shojaeinasab [19] concentrates on forensic detection using
address graph analysis and machine learning. The study briefly
acknowledges key laundering infrastructures—mixers, AECs,
exchanges, and PCNs, but does not attempt a formal categorization of laundering strategies or mechanisms. Its primary
contribution lies in detection rather than systematization.
Sneck [15] presents a systematic literature review of
cryptocurrency-enabled laundering and terrorist financing. The
work touches on several components of our taxonomy, including mixers, privacy coins, exchanges, chain-hopping, NFTs,
and regulatory arbitrage. However, discussions included in
the paper are example-driven and fail to formalize laundering
mechanisms or attacker strategies. The absence of a structured
taxonomy limits its utility for analytics or forensics.
Almeida et al. [16] are among the few sources that attempt a structured classification of laundering methods by
mapping them to PLI stages. They discuss several practical
techniques which include in-person and P2P transactions,
cryptocurrency ATMs, gambling, decentralized exchanges, and
mixers. However, their categorization lacks granularity, omits
many modern Web3 laundering mechanisms, and provides
only brief descriptions of each tactic. Our work complements
and extends their stage-based view by introducing a twodimensional taxonomy encompassing both laundering intent
and intermediary implementation.
Comolli and Korver [13] provide a narrative overview of
various laundering techniques and enforcement challenges in
Web3. They refer to several elements also contained in our
taxonomy such as commingling, mixers, jurisdictional arbitrage, and exchanges, while also touching on chain-hopping
via atomic swaps and DEXs. However, their analysis does not
differentiate strategies from mechanisms, nor does it cover
emerging techniques such as cross-chain bridges, consensus
participation, or NFT-based laundering. Our taxonomy refines
and extends an unstructured list of laundering tools into a
coherent framework.

In contrast to all prior work, our study introduces a unified
two-dimensional taxonomy that separates laundering strategies
from their enabling mechanisms and maps them to the stages
of the laundering lifecycle. We further identify the nature of
forensic traces they leave—whether on-chain, off-chain, or
cross-chain—enabling a more operationally useful classification. Our approach is grounded in qualitative thematic analysis
and conceptual clustering, drawing from academic literature,
regulatory reports, and forensic case studies. This allows us
to capture under-explored techniques such as laundering via
participation in mining and validating transactions, which are
absent from mentioned sources.
